item.title: Canada-U.S. talks gain more momentum ahead of midterms: sources
item.description: Multiple government and industry sources close to trade discussions between Canada and the United States tell CTV News the momentum of the talks, just recently re-started in earnest, combined with U.S ...
item.dc:creator: Vassy Kapelos, Marieke Walsh, Graham Richardson, Mike Le Couteur
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA – Multiple government and industry sources close to trade discussions between Canada and the United States tell CTV News the momentum of the talks, just recently re-started in earnest, combined with U.S. President Donald Trump’s political vulnerabilities ahead of the midterms leads them to believe there is considerable appetite from the White House to strike a deal with Canada. All the sources cautioned an agreement of any sort was far from certain given the past behaviour of Trump and his trade delegates including U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. But, over the last week the White House has shown much more interest in arriving at an agreement “than in all the weeks prior,” according to one of the sources, who also intimated progress on auto tariffs looked possible relative to where things were at when talks broke down in August. At a rally in Michigan Sunday, Trump referenced the closure of car plants in Canada and Mexico, insisting without providing evidence, that “Canada has been ripping off the United States for years. We’ll have that settled really soon; they’re willing to give us anything at this moment.” Asked late last week while in Turkiye whether a deal with the U.S. was suddenly possible, based on what sources were telling CTV News, Prime Minister Mark Carney said it would be up to the U.S. “They’re a little hard to predict,” Carney said Friday. “We’re ready to drop everything, sit down, and negotiate this afternoon if the Americans are ready in good faith.” Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc was supposed to be in his New Brunswick riding on Friday for an announcement but cancelled to stay in Ottawa. Approached by a CTV News reporter in the downtown core, the minister would not explain why he remained in Ottawa. Two sources described intense talks over the weekend, that were “all consuming.” Another source with knowledge of talks on both sides of the border said things are moving. Reached for comment Sunday, LeBlanc’s spokesperson Eve Giroux-Loignon wrote in a statement, “Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities,” adding “we stand ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests.” White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett told Fox News Sunday morning the U.S. was close to a deal with Canada and that talks are “gathering steam.” Trump’s U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer last month insisted Trump felt “no urgency” to make a deal with Canada. The president is facing lagging polls just 10 days out from U.S. midterm elections, which put his party in a position to lose the House and potentially the Senate as well. The escalating cost of living has become a defining issue in the elections. There are two factors driving up prices: the war in Iran and Trump’s tariff policy. In some senate races - Michigan and Maine are two examples - tariffs on Canada are the core election issue. Evidence of that materialized Friday, when the White House announced it would remove some tariffs on Canada, adding less consequential ones, in a bid to boost embattled Republican Senator Susan Collins’ campaign for re-election. Collins took credit for the tariff changes, writing in a statement, “I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbor, ally, and largest trading partner.” Democrats slammed the president’s abrupt tariff about-face. The top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, Ron Wyden, said in a statement, “Trump’s desperate, 11th hour attempt to save Susan Collins’ political career is an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies.” Hours before making those changes, Trump claimed that Canada “very much wants to make a deal” with the U.S. to restore trade peace, while insisting “we have all the cards.” In August, Canadian and U.S. trade officials came very close to striking a deal, but the talks fell apart in the final hours. At the time Carney contended the Americans made last minute demands around French language and culture, critical minerals, autos and sovereignty that were untenable. “In short, they asked too much and offered too little,” Carney insisted at the time. The U.S. midterms are set to take place Nov. 3. With files from CTV News’ Stephanie Ha and Jeremie Charron

item.title: ‘They are the nicest people’: Barack Obama ridicules Trump’s trade war with Canada
item.description: Former U.S. president Barack Obama took aim at U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods Saturday during an impassioned speech at a Democrat campaign rally in Detroit, Michigan, ahead of ...
item.dc:creator: Archie Niari
item.content:encoded: Former U.S. president Barack Obama has turned Canada into the punchline of an attack on U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade policies, mocking his tariffs against one of America’s closest allies and warning that the measures are pushing prices higher for consumers. Speaking at a Democratic campaign rally in Detroit on Saturday, Obama sarcastically described Canada as a “well-known evil empire,” before pointing out how unusual it was for Washington to be at odds with its northern neighbour. The remarks come as Trump’s trade war with Canada remains a contentious issue ahead of next month’s U.S. midterm elections, with economic ties between the two countries particularly significant in Michigan, a major automotive manufacturing state where the automotive sector relies on deeply integrated supply chains connecting Canadian and American factories. Obama argued that tariffs were working against Trump’s promises to bring down prices, particularly in an industry where manufacturing depends on parts moving across the Canada-U.S. border. In his speech, Obama noted that building a vehicle involves components sourced from multiple locations in both countries, meaning tariffs can raise costs throughout the production process rather than simply making imported goods more expensive. “He was warned,” Obama said of Trump’s tariff policy. “This will drive prices up. This does not lower prices.” Obama also mocked the deterioration in relations between the two countries, highlighting Canada’s proximity to the United States and its cultural contributions. “These are the people who gave us Martin Short … and maple syrup,” he said, describing Canadians as among the nicest people. He suggested Trump’s repeated threats to annex Canada and make it the 51st U.S. state, alongside his trade measures, had helped fuel Canadian anger toward Washington. The former U.S. president’s comments come amid a widening trade dispute that has affected a range of Canadian industries, including steel, aluminum, lumber and automotive manufacturing. Canada has responded to U.S. trade measures with counter-tariffs, adding pressure to a relationship that supports businesses, workers and consumers on both sides of the border. Obama also linked the tariff debate to the broader affordability challenge facing Americans, arguing that Trump’s approach had failed to deliver the lower prices he promised. With files from The Canadian Press

item.title: Wall Street mostly loses ground under pressure from rising oil prices
item.description: Futures are lower as oil prices reach levels not seen since May amid halting efforts to bring the U.S. and Iran back to the negotiation table.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Stocks on Wall Street closed broadly lower Friday as oil prices climbed to their highest level in more than four years, ratcheting up pressure on the market. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent, adding to its decline from a day before. The index posted its second-straight weekly loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after giving up a modest gain. Rising oil prices weighed heavily on the market, where nearly three out of every four stocks within the benchmark S&P 500 index fell. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 3.1 per cent to settle at US$116.72. It has surged from less than US$97 at the start of October and is now at its highest level since June 2022. Several AI-related companies rallied, helping ease some of the impact from the broader market slide. Micron Technology rose 2.5 per cent, Intel gained 1.7 per cent, Microsoft added 0.7 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices closed 1.7 per cent higher. The tech sector’s influence is also capable of quickly switching over to a heavy weight. Stocks that have benefited from the frenzy over AI have been swinging over rising worries about their path ahead. Investors are worried about whether their high prices are justified. Many of those companies have been borrowing to fund investments in AI technology and high interest rates are making those loans more expensive. “Investors appear increasingly focused on the economics of AI, particularly the substantial upfront costs required to build AI infrastructure and the uncertainty around the timing of returns on those investments,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note. The latest round of corporate earnings are being closely watched to help get a better sense of whether those investments are paying off, or might pay off. Several influential AI-related companies report their latest financial results next week, including Google’s parent, Alphabet, along with Microsoft and Amazon. Industrial companies had some of the biggest losses. Caterpillar fell 2.4 per cent. American Express slumped 3.7 per cent, one of several financial stocks that lost ground, despite r eporting profits for its most recent quarter that beat analysts’ forecasts. The company did announce its first major job cuts in roughly a decade. JPMorgan Chase fell 1.5 per cent, Citigroup dropped 1.5 per cent and Capital One Financial slid 1 per cent. While higher oil prices weighed down much of the market, they helped boost energy companies. Chevron rose 2.9 per cent and ConocoPhillips gained 3.6 per cent. European markets closed mostly lower. France’s main index fell 0.4 per cent, though yields on French government bonds eased a bit. Treasury yields in the U.S. edged higher following sharp drops on Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.99 per cent from 4.96 per cent late Thursday. Yields have been rising globally, partly over worries about governments taking on too much debt. Inflation also remains a concern and is stubbornly well above 3 per cent in the U.S. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation. Wall Street expects the central bank to hold rates steady at its meeting next week, but is leaning heavily toward another rate hike in December. Wall Street will also get several big economic updates next week, including the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. The personal consumption expenditures index, or PCE, is expected to show that inflation rose at a 3.7 per cent rate in September, sharply above the Fed’s 2 per cent target. The U.S. war with Iran has severely cut the world’s oil supply, driving energy prices higher and fueling a sharp jump in the cost of everything from gasoline to food and clothes. All told, the S&P 500 fell 39.75 points to 7,623.68. The Dow dropped 652.82 points to 52,215.16, and the Nasdaq gave up 53.52 points to close at 25,955.34. --- Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press
